Bachelor Degree Program in Computing and Artificial Intelligence (2018).

University: Cairo University.
Faculty: Computing and Artificial Intelligence.
Accredited by NAQAAE.

Faculty Vision:

To be the best source locally and regionally for academic education, scientific and applied research in the fields of computing, informatics, decision support, and artificial intelligence.

Faculty Mission:

The Faculty of Computers and Artificial Intelligence – Cairo University is committed to providing quality education and research to create a highly competitive cadre of specialists in the fields of informatics, computing, and decision support. The faculty also provides capacity building programs and offers consultancy and technical solutions that contribute to social and economic development.

Governing Values of the Faculty:

The values governing the performance of the faculty are represented by the acronym MATCH:

1. Market Oriented
2. Accountability
3. Transparency
4. Competitiveness
5. Academic Honesty

Faculty Objectives:

1. Raise the skills of graduates and increase the competitiveness of students and researchers.
2. Continuously develop the capabilities of faculty members and their assistants.
3. Provide a standard environment and an ideal climate for education and research.
4. Develop, support, and invest in promoting local and regional public and governmental services.
5. Strengthen partnerships with civil society institutions and support environmental development.
6. Commit to applying quality standards and periodically evaluating institutional capacity and educational effectiveness.

Objectives of the Bylaw Amendment:

The amendment of the faculty bylaws aims to:

1. Build an advanced educational system compatible with the rapid growth in computing and information fields.
2. Keep pace with modern scientific trends by updating study curricula.
3. Provide more opportunities for advanced practical training aligned with labor market requirements.
4. Allow students to choose majors according to their interests and preferences.
5. Provide an appropriate scientific environment for faculty members and researchers to pursue advanced scientific disciplines.
6. Enable students with different abilities to achieve their scientific ambitions and distinguish themselves academically.

General Framework of the Programs:

The Faculty of Computing and Artificial Intelligence accepts students who have obtained the General Secondary Certificate (Mathematics section) or an equivalent qualification in the same academic year through the Universities Admission Coordination Office.

The offered programs follow the credit hour system and are organized into four academic years, typically consisting of two regular semesters per academic year. A summer semester may also be offered when needed.

Study Plan Principles:

The study plan of the Faculty follows the credit hour system while maintaining internationally recognized academic standards. The plan is designed according to the following principles:

1. Adherence to international standards when selecting and distributing course percentages.
2. Openness to international academic practices.
3. Compliance with the National Academic Reference Standards (NARS) for Computing and Information (October 2010).

Article (1): Study Regulations

The offered programs are based on the Credit Hour System. The academic year consists of two regular semesters, and the credit hour is the unit used to measure the academic weight of a course.

Article (1): Summer Semester

The Faculty Council may approve intensive summer courses based on the recommendation of the scientific departments and according to the faculty's available resources and regulations.

Article (1): Graduation Requirements

To obtain the Bachelor of Computing and Artificial Intelligence degree, a student must successfully complete 135 credit hours over at least eight regular semesters, distributed across four academic levels.

Article (2): Language of Instruction

Courses in the offered programs may be taught in either Arabic or English depending on the requirements and nature of each course.

Article (3): Academic Advising

Each group of students is assigned an academic advisor from the faculty members. The academic advisor assists students in selecting courses, provides academic guidance throughout their studies, and helps them make informed academic decisions.

The advisor's recommendations are advisory only. Students are ultimately responsible for the courses they register for.

Article (4): Course Registration

At the beginning of each semester, students register their selected courses through the faculty website during the announced registration period.

Registration schedule:
- First week: Regular registration.
- Second week: Late registration with a financial penalty.
- Third and fourth weeks: Course withdrawal period.

The Faculty Council determines the minimum and maximum number of students allowed to enroll in each course.

Article (4): Registration Credit Hours for Regular Semesters

Registration rules for regular semesters are as follows:

- Minimum registration load: 9 credit hours. This minimum may be waived if the student needs fewer than 9 credit hours to graduate.
- Students with GPA ≥ 2.00 may register up to 18 credit hours.
- Students with GPA > 1.00 and < 2.00 may register up to 15 credit hours.
- Students with GPA ≤ 1.00 may register up to 12 credit hours.
- The maximum may be increased to 21 credit hours for students expected to graduate, subject to faculty approval.

Article (4): Summer Semester Registration Rules

The summer semester is an intensive seven-week semester in which the weekly teaching hours of each course are doubled.

- Maximum registration load: 6 credit hours.
- The maximum may be increased to 9 credit hours for graduation purposes, subject to faculty approval.

Article (4): Add and Drop Period

After completing course registration, students may add or drop one or more courses during the period specified by the faculty. The process is completed through the faculty website in coordination with the student's academic advisor.

Article (4): Prerequisite Rules

Students may register for higher-level courses according to the prerequisite structure of the curriculum. A student cannot enroll in a course unless all of its prerequisite courses have been successfully completed.

Article (5): Course Withdrawal

A student may withdraw from one or more registered courses during the withdrawal period specified in Article (4), provided that the remaining registered credit hours do not fall below the minimum registration requirement for the semester.

In this case, the student receives a grade of 'W' (Withdrawn), and the course is not considered failed.

Article (5): Late Withdrawal

If a student withdraws from one or more courses after the official withdrawal period without a compelling excuse approved by the Faculty Council, the student receives a grade of 'F' in the withdrawn course(s).

Article (6): Attendance Policy

Attendance is mandatory in all programs. The faculty does not permit the affiliation system. Student attendance is monitored according to the regulations established by the Faculty Administration.

Article (6): Attendance Requirements

Students must attend at least 75% of lectures and practical sessions in every course.

If a student's absence exceeds 25% without an accepted excuse, the Faculty Council may prevent the student from taking the final examination and assign a score of zero in the final exam.

If an acceptable excuse is approved by the Faculty Council, the student receives a grade of 'W' (Withdrawn) instead.

Article (6): Absence from Final Examination

A student who is absent from the final examination without an accepted excuse receives a score of zero in the final exam and must repeat the course.

Article (6): Incomplete Grade (I)

If a student submits a compelling excuse accepted by the Faculty Council before or within two days after the final examination, the student may receive an 'I' (Incomplete) grade, provided that:

- The student earned at least 60% of the semester work marks.
- The student was not prevented from taking the final examination due to attendance.

The student is allowed to sit only for the final examination, and the final course grade is calculated by combining the previously earned semester work marks with the new final examination score.

The final examination must be completed within the same academic year or the following academic year; otherwise, the student must repeat the course and the previous semester work grades are discarded.

Article (6): Excused Absence Without Meeting Incomplete Requirements

If a student's excuse for missing the final examination is accepted but the student did not obtain at least 60% of the semester work marks, the student receives a grade of 'W' (Withdrawn) for the course.

Article (7): Suspension and Interruption of Study

A student is considered to have interrupted their studies if they fail to register for a semester or withdraw from all registered courses without an accepted excuse. Such a semester counts toward the maximum allowed study duration.

With an accepted excuse, a student may suspend studies for:

- Up to two consecutive semesters, or
- Up to three non-consecutive semesters.

Students may also apply for suspension of enrollment according to the university's regulations.

Article (8): Dismissal from the Faculty

Students are dismissed according to the maximum number of study years permitted under the Executive Regulations of the Universities Organization Law.

The maximum study duration is:

- First Level: 2 years.
- Second Level: 2 years plus one exceptional year with Faculty Council approval.
- Third Level: 2 years plus three exceptional years with Faculty Council approval.
- Fourth Level: 2 years plus three exceptional years with Faculty Council approval.

Approved suspension periods are not counted toward these limits.

Article (9): Examination System

The maximum score for any course is 100 marks.

To pass a course, a student must:

- Obtain at least 50% of the total course marks.
- Obtain at least 30% of the final examination marks.

Article (9): Grade Distribution

Course grades are distributed as follows:

Semester Work: 40%
- Midterm examination: up to 20%.
- Periodic quizzes.
- Practical work and assignments.
- Oral examinations may also be included.

Final Examination: 60%.

The Faculty Council determines and announces the schedules for midterm and final examinations.

Article (9): Written and Practical Final Examinations

For courses whose final assessment includes both written and practical examinations, the final examination score is calculated as the sum of the written examination marks and the practical examination marks, subject to approval by the department councils and the Faculty Council.

Article (10): Evaluation System

The Faculty follows the credit-hour system, where the course—not the academic year—is the fundamental unit of evaluation. Each course is assigned a letter grade and corresponding grade points based on the student's final percentage.

Grade Scale:
- A+ : 90% or above → 4.0 points
- A  : 85% to less than 90% → 3.7 points
- B+ : 80% to less than 85% → 3.3 points
- B  : 75% to less than 80% → 3.0 points
- C+ : 70% to less than 75% → 2.7 points
- C  : 65% to less than 70% → 2.4 points
- D+ : 60% to less than 65% → 2.2 points
- D  : 50% to less than 60% → 2.0 points
- F  : Less than 50% → 0.0 points.

Article (10): GPA Calculation

The cumulative Grade Point Average (GPA) is calculated by multiplying the grade points earned in each course by the course's credit hours to obtain total points. The points from all registered courses are summed and divided by the total registered credit hours.

Formula:
GPA = Total Grade Points / Total Registered Credit Hours.

Article (10): Overall Academic Standing

The student's overall academic standing is determined according to the cumulative GPA:

- GPA below 1.5 → Very Poor
- GPA from 1.5 to less than 2.0 → Poor
- GPA from 2.0 to less than 2.5 → Acceptable
- GPA from 2.5 to less than 3.0 → Good
- GPA from 3.0 to less than 3.5 → Very Good
- GPA of 3.5 or above → Excellent.

Article (10): Graduation with Honors

A student is awarded graduation honors if all of the following conditions are met:

1. The student passes all courses at every academic level with an overall grade of at least Very Good.
2. The total study period does not exceed four academic years.
3. The student has never failed, been deprived from an examination, or repeated a course during study at the Faculty or any faculty from which the student transferred.

Article (11): Failure and Repeating Courses

If a student fails a course, the student must re-study the course and take the examination again. If the student passes after repeating the course, the actual grade obtained will be recorded, but the maximum grade that can be counted is D+ (64 marks). The student's cumulative GPA is calculated based on this capped grade.

Article (12): Department Responsibilities and Course Regulations

Each academic department is responsible for preparing a complete description of the courses it offers. After approval by the Faculty Council, the approved course descriptions become mandatory for all faculty members teaching those courses.

Upon the recommendation of the relevant department councils, the Faculty Council may modify the prerequisite requirements for any course and may also update the scientific content of a course, provided that the changes do not exceed 25% of the core course content.

Article (13): Academic Level Progression

Students are assigned to academic levels based on the total number of successfully completed credit hours:

• First Level: Upon admission and until completing fewer than 27 credit hours.
• Second Level: After successfully completing at least 27 credit hours.
• Third Level: After successfully completing at least 60 credit hours.
• Fourth Level: After successfully completing at least 96 credit hours.

Article (14): Application of the Regulations

1. The provisions of this regulation apply to all newly admitted students starting from the academic year following the approval of the regulation.
2. In cases where this regulation does not explicitly provide a rule, the provisions of the Universities Organization Law and its Executive Regulations shall apply.

Article (15): Course Code Structure

The code of every course consists of the code of the department offering the course, followed by a three-digit number.

The three digits have the following meaning:

• The hundreds digit represents the academic level.
• The tens digit represents the exact specialization of the course within the department.
• The ones digit distinguishes different courses within the same specialization and academic level.

Article (15): Department Code Symbols

The symbolic codes for departments are:

• Computer Science Department: Arabic "علح" — English "CS".

Specialization Requirements (63 Credit Hours)

Computer Science Program specialization requirements consist of 63 credit hours divided into:

1. Applied Sciences – Compulsory Courses (39 Credit Hours).
2. Applied Sciences – Elective Courses (18 Credit Hours).
3. Graduation Project (6 Credit Hours).

Compulsory specialization courses are classified as Type (D). Elective specialization courses are classified as Type (G) or Type (D), depending on the course. Every specialization course carries 3 credit hours, distributed into 2.5 lecture hours and 1.5 laboratory/tutorial hours per week.
